Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

issues.explanation: The trigger set is mostly coherent with rape trauma (locked/confined spaces, sexual-violence comments), but sirens are hard to connect to the rest of this profile and trauma context. With strong Negative Appraisals↔Threat and links from both to Triggers, the triggers should plausibly cue the patient's threat meanings; sirens do not fit the sexual-assault/confinement theme represented by the other trigger and appraisal items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilant unsafe-world items (back to wall, staying alert to sleep) fit well, but 'taking too many risks' pulls in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile with the same immediate threat style. It also lacks support elsewhere in the profile, since no other items suggest disinhibition, anger, numbing, or self-destructive coping.

vignette:
Darnell had been assaulted in a way that left the ordinary boundaries of a room feeling permanently altered. The rape had happened after he was cornered in a locked office by a man he knew only casually, someone who had seemed unthreatening enough before the door clicked shut and the space turned, in an instant, from private to trapped. In the months that followed, Darnell, a 37-year-old psychologist who lived alone and worked in a busy outpatient clinic, found that anything resembling that helpless enclosure could pull him back into the same state of dread: a small consultation room with the door closed, the awkward quiet of being alone with a male patient, or a colleague’s casual remark about sexual violence on a training day. He noticed how quickly his body reacted before he could think, as if his mind had already decided that locked spaces and sexual talk were warnings, not coincidences.

What frightened Darnell most was the conclusion he had come to about himself. He had become convinced that he had no future worth imagining and that nothing he did could stop bad things from happening to him. He often felt that other people could somehow see what had happened just by looking at him, as though the assault had left a mark on his face or in his posture. Those thoughts made him scan every room for escape routes and placement, choosing a seat only if he could keep his back against a wall and see the whole space. He could not relax, even in his own apartment, because the sense of being exposed seemed to follow him from place to place; and the more he felt trapped by the belief that danger would come regardless, the more those same locked doors, male voices, and sexual references took on the force of personal threats.

At work, the pattern had become especially costly. Darnell began arriving early so he could choose the office chair farthest from the door and angle himself where no one could come up behind him. If a male client was waiting and the receptionist asked him to close the door for confidentiality, his chest tightened and he would feel forced to decide between professional composure and the urge to keep the room open. He started avoiding the smaller therapy rooms altogether and would sometimes ask a colleague to sit in on sessions without fully explaining why. When a coworker made an offhand comment about a news story involving sexual violence, he went abruptly silent and later found himself checking the locks on his office door twice before he could settle enough to continue seeing patients. The more these moments accumulated, the more certain he became that his own life was narrowing, that he had no future beyond managing fear, and that his inability to keep danger away was proof he had already been defeated.

Sleep had become another place where his vigilance would not let him go. Darnell described lying in bed with his mind fixed on sounds in the hallway, on whether the apartment door was properly secured, on whether he had chosen a position that would let him see an intruder if one came in. He delayed sleep because he felt he had to stay alert, and when he finally lay down, he often felt unable to relax at all. The restless nights fed back into the next day’s fear; the exhaustion made him feel even more vulnerable, which in turn sharpened his conviction that he was exposed and unprotected. That sense of constant alertness also made the triggers feel closer and more frequent, so that any closed door, any unexpected comment about rape, any time he found himself alone with a man in the clinic corridor could set off the same tightening wave of danger.

Over time, Darnell’s world had grown smaller. He declined invitations to meet friends in apartments with limited exits, chose restaurants with open seating, and arranged his schedule around avoiding situations where he would be alone with men he did not know well. He had come for help now because he was tired of organizing every day around fear and because his work, the one place he had once felt most competent, was beginning to feel governed by the same trapped, watchful state. He was most afraid that if he did not find a way to loosen the grip of these beliefs, he would spend the rest of his life living as though the assault were still happening, unable to rest, unable to trust safety even when it was right in front of him.
